prompt: Who are the twelve factors rules for, according to the lesson?
hint: What does a platform do to the program without asking?

choices.text: Applications deployed to Heroku, and nowhere else
choices.why: They came from Heroku and apply far beyond it.

choices.text: Microservices only, since a monolith has nothing to scale
choices.why: The monolith of lesson 1 is started and stopped by a platform too.

choices.text: Any program a platform starts, stops, copies and moves
choices.why: Right, a monolith or a function as much as a service.

choices.text: Programs written in Ruby, the language Heroku began with
choices.why: Nothing in the factors is about a language.

prompt: Match each factor to what it asks.
hint: The table in the first section.

pairs.right: what differs between deploys lives in the environment
keep nothing between requests that another needs
one stream of events on standard output

prompt: The twelve factors were written down in 2011 by Adam Wiggins, one of the founders of ___.
hint: A platform where developers pushed code and never saw the machines.

prompt: `requirements.txt` lists only `psycopg[binary]==3.3.6`, and `pip freeze` shows three packages. What does that say about pinning?
hint: Who chose the versions of the other two?

choices.text: Only the top level is pinned
choices.why: Right. `typing_extensions` is free to change between two builds; a lock file pins the whole tree.

choices.text: Pip ignored the pin and installed extra packages
choices.why: Pip installed what the pinned package depends on.

choices.text: Every package must be written by hand in the file, or the build fails
choices.why: The build worked; the risk is drift, not failure.

choices.text: The image contains packages from the machine it was built on
choices.why: The image installed only from the list, inside the build.

prompt: What does factor I, codebase, forbid?
hint: One codebase, many deploys.

choices.text: Several programs in one repository
choices.why: A monorepo is fine.

choices.text: Production code kept in its own repository
choices.why: Right. The two drift and nobody knows which is running.

choices.text: Deploying the same commit to staging and production
choices.why: That is exactly what the factor asks for.

choices.text: More than one branch in the repository
choices.why: Branches are fine; deploys come from one codebase.

prompt: Why does the Dockerfile copy `requirements.txt` and install it before copying `catalogue.py`?
hint: What does a change to the code invalidate?

choices.text: Pip refuses to install while a .py file is present
choices.why: Pip does not care what else is in the directory.

choices.text: The program must be the last layer for Python to find it
choices.why: Python finds it wherever it is copied.

choices.text: A code change then reuses the cached dependency layer
choices.why: Right: the slow `pip install` runs only when the list changes.

choices.text: It keeps the dependencies out of the final image
choices.why: They are in the image; that is the point of II.

prompt: Which of these is config, in the sense of factor III?
hint: Does it change between deploys of the same code?

choices.text: The list of routes the catalogue answers
choices.why: Routes are the same everywhere; they are code.

choices.text: The rule that a basket over 5 kg pays more
choices.why: A business rule is code.

choices.text: The database's address
choices.why: Right. It differs between laptop, staging and production.

choices.text: The names of the five products
choices.why: The products are data, created by the migration, not config.

prompt: Started with `DATABASE_URL` empty, the catalogue exits with code 1 and a sentence. Why is that better than starting with a default address?
hint: When, and in front of whom, does each one fail?

choices.text: A default would make the program slower to start
choices.why: Speed is not the argument.

choices.text: It fails in the deploy, while somebody is watching
choices.why: Right. A default would fail later, on a real request, naming a host nobody configured.

choices.text: Exit code 1 restarts the container with the right value
choices.why: Nothing supplies the right value; the person deploying has to.

choices.text: Defaults are forbidden by the twelve factors
choices.why: `PORT` has a default, and the lesson approves of it.

prompt: What is the test the twelve-factor text gives for whether config is properly separated from code?
hint: Publishing the code.

choices.text: Every setting has a default value written in the code
choices.why: Defaults are config in the code, which is the problem.

choices.text: The program reads a config file at start-up, kept with the code
choices.why: A committed file with credentials fails the test.

choices.text: Publishing the code would leak no credential
choices.why: Right: as open source, today, with nothing removed.

choices.text: The program runs on a laptop with no network
choices.why: That is about dependencies and backing services, not config.

prompt: A team puts the payment gateway's secret key in an environment variable and calls it done. What does the lesson add?
hint: Where it is handed over, and where it lives.

choices.text: Environment variables are encrypted by Docker, so it is safe
choices.why: Docker does not encrypt them; `docker inspect` prints them.

choices.text: Secrets must be compiled into the image instead
choices.why: That puts the secret in every copy of the image, everywhere.

choices.text: Secrets belong in a committed file
choices.why: That fails the open-source test.

choices.text: Store it in a vault that hands it over at start-up
choices.why: Right: a secret manager injects it and keeps an audit of who read it, with no change to the program.

prompt: What did it take to move the catalogue from `db` to `other-db`?
hint: Look at the command that recreated it.

choices.text: A rebuild of the image with a new hostname
choices.why: The image was the same; nothing was rebuilt.

choices.text: Another `DATABASE_URL`
choices.why: Right, and the migration run against the new database. The code did not change.

choices.text: Copying the data from one database to the other first
choices.why: The new one started empty, which is why the first request failed.

choices.text: Editing `catalogue.py` to point at the new host
choices.why: The host is never named in the code.

prompt: Right after the catalogue was pointed at `other-db`, its request failed. Why?
hint: What was in the new database?

choices.text: The URL was wrong, so the connection was refused
choices.why: The connection worked; the query found no table.

choices.text: PostgreSQL 17 cannot be used by two containers
choices.why: Two containers can use it; this was a different database.

choices.text: The catalogue keeps the old database open until restarted
choices.why: It opens a connection per request, to whatever the URL names.

choices.text: The new database had no `products` table yet
choices.why: Right. The admin task had not run against it.

prompt: Why did the catalogue answer on a different port after it was recreated?
hint: Look at the ports line of `compose.yaml`.

choices.text: The program chose a random port when it started
choices.why: It always listens on `PORT`, 8000, inside the container.

choices.text: Docker gave it a free port from the range
choices.why: Right. The platform decides the outside port; `docker compose port` says which.

choices.text: The database told it to move
choices.why: A database has no say in the catalogue's port.

choices.text: Port 8000 was blocked by a firewall rule
choices.why: Nothing blocked it; another port was simply picked.

prompt: The team swaps PostgreSQL for MySQL by changing `DATABASE_URL`. What does the lesson say about that?
hint: Where the resource is, against what it is.

choices.text: The URL says where a resource is, not what it is
choices.why: Right. A program written for PostgreSQL does not run on MySQL because a URL changed.

choices.text: It works, because the factor guarantees any database can be swapped
choices.why: The factor promises no such thing.

choices.text: It works if the image is rebuilt with the new driver
choices.why: A new driver does not make the SQL dialects the same.

choices.text: It is forbidden, because backing services must never change
choices.why: Changing the attached resource is what the factor makes easy.

prompt: In the twelve factors, what is a release?
hint: Two things combined, and then frozen.

choices.text: A new commit pushed to the main branch
choices.why: A commit is code; the build has not happened yet.

choices.text: The image, before it is configured
choices.why: That is the build.

choices.text: One build plus one environment's config
choices.why: Right, numbered and never changed.

choices.text: The processes running in production
choices.why: Those are the run stage.

prompt: Production misbehaves after release 42. What does a rollback do, in this model?
hint: Does anything get built?

choices.text: Builds the previous commit again and deploys it
choices.why: A rollback never builds; the earlier release still exists.

choices.text: Edits the running code on the server to undo the change
choices.why: Editing running code is what the factor forbids.

choices.text: Starts the processes of release 41 again
choices.why: Right, exactly as it was.

choices.text: Deletes release 42 so that it cannot be used
choices.why: Deleting is not the rollback; starting the earlier one is.

prompt: Why does the lesson tag the existing image as 1.0.0 instead of building again with `TAG=1.0.0`?
hint: Is a second build the same artefact?

choices.text: `docker tag` is faster than a build on every machine
choices.why: Speed is not the argument.

choices.text: Compose cannot build images with a tag
choices.why: It can; `image:` with `${TAG}` does exactly that.

choices.text: Tags created by `docker tag` cannot be moved later
choices.why: Any tag can be moved, which is why releases pin digests.

choices.text: A second build is a second artefact
choices.why: Right, and not the one that was tested. Build once, name it, release it.

prompt: Why does a real release pin an image by digest rather than by tag?
hint: Which of the two can point somewhere else tomorrow?

choices.text: A digest is shorter to type
choices.why: A digest is long; that is not the reason.

choices.text: Only a digest names one build for ever
choices.why: Right. A tag can be moved to another image later, and a release must keep naming exactly one build.

choices.text: Registries delete images that are referred to only by tag
choices.why: Registries keep tagged images.

choices.text: Tags are not allowed in production by Docker
choices.why: Docker allows tags anywhere.

prompt: After five requests to `/hits` spread over three copies, the first copy answered 3. What did each of the other two answer?
hint: Each counts only what it saw.

prompt: Why were the products the same in all three copies when the hit counts were not?
hint: Where does each answer come from?

choices.text: The products are cached in each copy at start-up
choices.why: They are read from the database on every request.

choices.text: One comes from the database, the other from memory
choices.why: Right. What must be the same for every copy lives in a backing service.

choices.text: The load balancer sends product requests to one copy only
choices.why: There is no load balancer; each copy was asked directly.

choices.text: Counting requests is not supported by Python's HTTP server
choices.why: It counts them fine, in the wrong place.

prompt: A shop keeps each user's basket in the memory of the process that served them, and turns on sticky sessions. What breaks it?
hint: What does the platform do without asking?

choices.text: A user opening the shop in two tabs
choices.why: Both tabs reach the same copy with sticky sessions.

choices.text: Too many products in one basket
choices.why: Size is not the issue.

choices.text: That copy restarting, being replaced or scaled away
choices.why: Right: the basket goes with it.

choices.text: The database going down for a minute
choices.why: The basket was never in the database.

prompt: Match each factor to what the lab did to show it.
hint: The section groups three factors.

pairs.right: Docker chose which port of the range each copy got

right_distractors: `docker tag` gave the build a second name

prompt: How many seconds does Docker wait after SIGTERM before sending SIGKILL, by default?
hint: The sleeper took a little over this.

prompt: The one-line sleeper ignored SIGTERM although Python normally exits on it. Why?
hint: Which process was it, inside the container?

choices.text: Python ignores every signal while it is sleeping in time.sleep
choices.why: A Python process outside a container exits on SIGTERM while sleeping.

choices.text: Docker never sends SIGTERM to containers built from Python images
choices.why: Docker sends it to every container's first process.

choices.text: It was PID 1, which ignores signals it has no handler for
choices.why: Right. So Docker waited and then killed it.

choices.text: The `time.sleep` call blocks every signal for an hour
choices.why: Signals still arrive during sleep; nothing acted on this one.

prompt: Which of these stop a container from waiting out the grace period on SIGTERM? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three ways out are named.

choices.text: Handling SIGTERM in the program
choices.why: Right, as the catalogue does.

choices.text: Running with `docker run --init`
choices.why: Right: a small init forwards the signal.

choices.text: Raising the grace period to sixty seconds
choices.why: That makes the wait longer.

choices.text: Starting the program itself, not a shell script that swallows signals
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Writing logs to a file instead of standard output
choices.why: Logs have nothing to do with signals.

prompt: What happens to a request in progress when a server that ignores SIGTERM is stopped?
hint: How does the stop end?

choices.text: It finishes, because Docker waits for it
choices.why: Docker waits ten seconds, then kills, finished or not.

choices.text: It is cut off by SIGKILL at the end of the grace period
choices.why: Right, on every deploy.

choices.text: It is moved to another copy automatically
choices.why: Nothing moves a request between processes.

choices.text: It is retried by the server after it restarts
choices.why: The server does not keep requests to retry.

prompt: Where should the catalogue write its logs, according to factor XI?
hint: It does not know where they go.

choices.text: To `/var/log/catalogue.log`, inside the container
choices.why: That disk goes away with the container.

choices.text: To the database, in a logs table
choices.why: That ties logging to a backing service the logs should help debug.

choices.text: To standard output
choices.why: Right. Collecting and storing is the platform's job.

choices.text: To a file per day, rotated by the program
choices.why: Rotation is storage, which is not the program's job here.

prompt: Developers use SQLite on their laptops and production runs PostgreSQL. Which gap of factor X is that?
hint: Time, people or tools.

choices.text: Time
choices.why: Time is code written now and deployed weeks later.

choices.text: People
choices.why: People is who writes against who deploys.

choices.text: Tools
choices.why: Right. Containers make closing it cheap.

choices.text: None; SQLite and PostgreSQL behave the same
choices.why: They differ, for example in what an integer column accepts.

prompt: How does the lesson run the migration that creates the products table?
hint: Same image, same config, then it exits.

choices.text: From a SQL file on the developer's laptop, with psql
choices.why: A script on a laptop runs with the wrong dependencies sooner or later.

choices.text: Automatically, each time the service starts
choices.why: The service does not migrate; a separate one-off process does.

choices.text: As a one-off process: `docker compose run --rm`
choices.why: Right: factor XII.

choices.text: By an operator typing the CREATE TABLE in production
choices.why: That leaves no record and no repeatable step.

prompt: A service reads its database password from `config.py`, committed to the repository, and writes logs to `/app/logs/service.log`. Which factors does it break?
hint: One about where config lives, one about where logs go.

choices.text: I and II
choices.why: Codebase and dependencies are not the problem here.

choices.text: III and XI
choices.why: Right: config in the code, logs in a file.

choices.text: V and IX
choices.why: Neither releases nor stopping are described.

choices.text: VI and VIII
choices.why: Nothing is said about state or scaling.

prompt: Put the steps of shipping a fix to the catalogue in twelve-factor order.
hint: Build, release, run, and the commit before them.
trap: Editing the running code is not a step at all: a fix is always a new commit and a new release.
items: Build one image from that commit
Combine the image with production's config as a new release
Start processes from the release, stopping the old ones gracefully
